speaker: ALEX
text: Welcome back. Today we're looking at GitHub Gists, which are one of the lightest ways to share code, notes, examples, and small configuration files.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So not a whole project, not a full repository, just a quick shareable thing?

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. A Gist can hold one file or several files, and each file can have syntax highlighting if GitHub recognizes the extension. It's useful when you want to show a snippet, save a small note, or give someone a reproducible example without creating an entire repo.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I like that middle ground. Sometimes an issue comment is too cramped, but a new repository feels like overkill.

speaker: ALEX
text: That's where Gists fit nicely. They are small, linkable, and still connected to Git, so you can edit them and keep a history of changes.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The appendix that this episode goes with also talks about GitHub Discussions. Before we stay with Gists, can we place Discussions in the workflow?

speaker: ALEX
text: Sure. GitHub Discussions is the forum-style area for a repository or an organization. It is where questions, ideas, announcements, polls, and community Q&A can live without turning every conversation into an issue or pull request.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So an issue says, there is work to track. A discussion says, let's talk, ask, compare, or decide whether there should be work.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Use an issue for a bug, a specific feature request, or a task that needs labels, assignees, and closure. Use a discussion for questions, brainstorming, community input, or a topic that may not have one final answer.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the categories help set that expectation before anyone replies.

speaker: ALEX
text: They do. Common categories include Q&A for support questions, Ideas for brainstorming, Announcements for maintainer updates, General for everything else, and Show and Tell when community members share what they built.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Where does the workshop support hub fit into that?

speaker: ALEX
text: For alumni, the Community-Access/support repository is the ongoing support home. Read the pinned Start Here resources in Discussions, search existing threads before starting a new one, and use issues when you have a setup blocker or accessibility blocker that maintainers need to track. In Accessibility Agents work, remember that the catalog grows over time, so Discussions are a good place for questions and ideas, while issues are better for concrete changes.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If I'm on a repository page, how do I get to Discussions without hunting around forever?

speaker: ALEX
text: Look in the main repository navigation near Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, and Projects. If you use keyboard shortcuts, T can move through tab items, and K can help you find links such as Discussions. If the tab is missing, that usually means the maintainer has not enabled Discussions for that repository.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And organizations can have their own Discussions too, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. An organization can host community-wide conversations that are not tied to one repository. On a Discussions home page, categories are usually shown with headings, and a side panel may appear on the left or right depending on the width of the view. That panel can show category counts, pinned items, active discussions, and tags if the project uses them.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Creating one sounds similar to opening an issue, but with a category first.

speaker: ALEX
text: That's the key difference. Activate New discussion, choose a required category, write a clear searchable title, write the body in Markdown, and start the discussion. For Q&A, phrase the title as a real question, because that title becomes part of how other people search later.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should screen reader users expect in that form?

speaker: ALEX
text: The path is usually New discussion, category selection, title field, body editor, and Start discussion. The body editor behaves like an issue comment editor, so enter focus mode when your screen reader needs it, type your content, and Ctrl+Enter can submit. Inside a discussion, replies are often exposed as article elements; NVDA and JAWS users may use A to move among them, while VoiceOver users may prefer headings, links, or the rotor depending on browser setup.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And participation is more than just replying at the bottom.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. You can reply to the main thread, reply to a specific comment with a nested reply, upvote useful posts instead of adding plus-one comments, vote in polls, and, in Q&A threads, the discussion author can mark an accepted answer. Low-vision users may also notice answered badges, percentage bars after poll voting, and success banners that can appear above the current zoom position. If the interface changes, GitHub's own documentation is the reference to check.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Okay, back to Gists. If I want to make one from the web, where do I start?

speaker: ALEX
text: Go to gist.github.com while signed in. You'll get fields for an optional description, a filename, and the file contents. Name the file with a useful extension, like notes.md, example.py, or config.json, because that helps GitHub choose the right formatting.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And then I choose public or secret. This is the part where people can get surprised.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes, and it is important. A public Gist is visible and discoverable. A secret Gist is unlisted, meaning it is not meant to appear in public discovery, but anyone with the link can view it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So secret does not mean private.

speaker: ALEX
text: Correct. Don't put passwords, tokens, private keys, personal data, unreleased business information, or anything sensitive in a Gist. Treat secret Gist links as shareable links, not access control.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about multiple files? Can one Gist hold a small example with a script and a README?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Use Add file in the web interface and give each file its own name and content. That is handy for a short demo where you want a README, a code file, and maybe a sample output file all traveling together.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if I'm already in the terminal and I don't want to open the browser?

speaker: ALEX
text: If you use the GitHub CLI, you can create a Gist with gh gist create. For example, `gh gist create hello.py --public --desc 'small Python example'` creates a public Gist from that file with a short description.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if I want it unlisted instead?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the secret option when you mean unlisted, such as `gh gist create config.json notes.md --secret`. You can pass more than one filename, and the files become part of the same Gist. If you're piping text from another command, give the content a filename so people know what they're reading.

speaker: JAMIE
text: After the command runs, how do I know it worked?

speaker: ALEX
text: The CLI prints the Gist URL. Open that URL, check the filenames, read the rendered content, and make sure the visibility matches what you intended before sharing it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: You said earlier that Gists are connected to Git. Does that mean they have history like repositories?

speaker: ALEX
text: They do. A Gist is a Git repository behind the scenes, so edits create revisions. You can edit in the browser, review the revision history, and see what changed over time.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Can I clone one locally too?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. On the Gist page, copy the clone URL, or use the CLI with `gh gist clone` followed by the Gist identifier or URL. Once it's local, you can inspect the files in your editor, make changes, commit, and push if you have permission to update that Gist.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And comments live on the Gist page, not in my local clone.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Gist comments are for discussion around the snippet or note. To add one, open the Gist page, move to the comment editor near the bottom, type your message, and submit it much like an issue comment.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Gists also have stars and forks. Are those the same as repository stars and forks?

speaker: ALEX
text: Similar idea, smaller scale. Starring a Gist saves or signals appreciation for it. Forking a Gist makes your own copy under your account, so you can modify it without changing the original.

speaker: JAMIE
text: But I shouldn't expect the whole repository collaboration system.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. A Gist doesn't give you the same project structure, issue tracker, pull request workflow, releases, or automation that a full repository does. It is lightweight sharing, not a complete project home.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do I find my own Gists later?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the Gists area from your GitHub profile, go directly to gist.github.com, or visit gist.github.com followed by your username. Screen reader users can move by headings and links to the Gist list, then open titles. You can also browse public Gists through GitHub's Gist discovery areas or arrive at them through links, search results, and community posts.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Embedding sounds useful. What does it mean to embed a Gist in a web page?

speaker: ALEX
text: It means placing the Gist content inside another page, usually a blog post, lesson, or documentation page. On the Gist page, GitHub provides an embed script you can copy and paste into an HTML page.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the page shows the snippet without me re-copying all the code by hand.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes, and if you update the Gist, the embedded version can reflect that update. For accessibility, don't rely only on the embedded script. Add a short plain-language summary and a direct link to the Gist, so people have another route if scripts are blocked, slow, or awkward with their setup.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Give me a few situations where a Gist is the right tool.

speaker: ALEX
text: A good one is sharing screen reader configuration notes, like NVDA settings for GitHub web navigation. Another is a quick Markdown note, such as Workshop Day 1 notes, where the content is useful but not a project. A third is a code snippet for an answer on Stack Overflow or in a support thread.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And when should I stop and make a real repository instead?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use a repository when the work has a project shape: a README, folders, tests, issues, pull requests, releases, permissions, or ongoing collaboration. Use a Gist when the work is small, self-contained, and easy to understand as a snippet or note.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So a Gist is great for showing a pattern. A repository is better for maintaining a thing.

speaker: ALEX
text: Nicely put. If you expect other people to file bugs, propose changes, run workflows, or follow a roadmap, give the work a repository.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's end with the safety check, because secret Gists can sound safer than they are.

speaker: ALEX
text: They can, and the rule is simple: never put sensitive data in Gists. Public Gists are discoverable. Secret Gists are link-accessible. Neither one is a password vault.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If I accidentally put a token in a Gist and then delete the Gist, am I safe?

speaker: ALEX
text: No. If a secret or public value was exposed, rotate or revoke it as soon as possible. Deleting the Gist removes the page from your account, but you cannot assume nobody copied the content, cached it, or followed the link while it existed.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do I delete one when I really do want it gone?

speaker: ALEX
text: Open the Gist, find its delete control, confirm the deletion, and then verify it no longer appears in your Gists list. For routine cleanup, that's enough. For leaked secrets, cleanup is only the first step; revocation is the real fix.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the everyday workflow is: use Gists for small shareable material, be clear about visibility, and move to a repository when the work needs a real home.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Gists are small, but they're not throwaway. Used well, they make examples easier to share, easier to revise, and easier for someone else to understand.
